doc.title: Wayne Bergeron interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 29, 2020

title: Insisting on particular players and the power to say no
summary: Rowe asks about Henry Mancini demanding players; Bergeron talks about alternates and the value of being able to say no.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Would someone like Henry Mancini say I’m not doing this recording unless I get these four particular players? Would they hold the thing up until a time where all those people are available?

If he wanted that, of course they would. I mean most of the time they’ve got alternates. They go, oh man, Plas Johnson can’t do this one, you know, but we have to do this today. Who’s your next choice? Who do you like? You know such-and-such sounds like Plas you know, or we’ll get Pete Christlieb or whatever you know. So they probably do that. But there’s been times even in my thing where they’ve said — where I couldn’t be there and they’re writing for me and they’ve rescheduled the thing. That’s a kind of a good feeling to have.

It’s a powerful — in the music business it’s a very powerful thing to be able to say no, when you’re in a position to say no in any business it makes you more valuable, because you don’t need that. If you don’t need it, you know what I mean, if you don’t need that work or you don’t have to do this, and you say no, it’s a good — there’s something that feels good about that, especially in the music business because we’re so used to saying © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

yes to everything and being a slave to the music business. And like you said earlier, trying to make every session and make every call. And there’s a little bit of greed involved with that but there’s also a little bit of need involved with that because people need to make money. And that extra money can make or break some people. So you know, yeah.
